title: DHS Proposes $103,000 Fee for All H-1B Cap-Subject Petitions
excerpt: The proposed rule would codify the Trump administration's controversial H-1B fee as a permanent regulation, generating an estimated $8.8 billion annually.
body:
• DHS has published a proposed rule to permanently impose a $103,265 fee on all H-1B cap-subject petitions, including those filed under the advanced degree exemption
  • The fee would apply to new petitions, renewals, and F-1 students changing to H-1B status, but exempts cap-exempt employers such as universities and research organizations
  • A federal judge struck down the original $100,000 executive order fee in June 2026, and the First Circuit Court of Appeals is currently reviewing the case
  • The public has approximately 30 days to comment on the proposed rule, with the next H-1B cap season beginning in spring 2027

The Department of Homeland Security has proposed a regulation to permanently impose a $103,265 fee on every H-1B cap-subject petition filed with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, a move that would dramatically reshape the economics of hiring skilled foreign workers in the United States.

The proposed rule, published under docket number USCIS-2026-0298, would apply to all 85,000 annual cap-subject petitions — including those filed under the advanced degree exemption — and is projected to generate an estimated $8.8 billion in annual revenue for USCIS, according to the agency's own calculations.

From Executive Order to Permanent Rule

The proposed regulation seeks to codify on a permanent basis what began as an executive action. President Trump first imposed a $100,000 fee on H-1B petitions through Presidential Proclamation 10973 in September 2025, bypassing Congress entirely. That fee represented a staggering increase from the previous range of $2,000 to $5,000 that employers typically paid for H-1B filings.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=VVnGq-xv5TI

The legality of the executive order was immediately challenged in court. On June 8, 2026, U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin in Boston threw out the fee, ruling that the president lacked the authority to impose it and finding that only Congress can change immigration policy. The First Circuit Court of Appeals declined to reinstate the fee on July 24, leaving the executive order effectively dead.

"If an American corporation needs workers, it should hire and train Americans."

— JD Vance, Vice President of the United States

The proposed rule represents the administration's attempt to achieve the same outcome through the formal regulatory process, which carries greater legal durability than an executive order. USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler confirmed that the fee would be paid at the time of filing, in addition to all other existing petition fees.

Who Pays — and Who Doesn't

The proposed fee casts a wide net. It would apply not only to new H-1B petitions but also to foreign nationals already in the United States on student visas seeking to change their status, as well as those filing for renewals. This means F-1 visa holders — many of whom are Indian students at American universities — would face the fee when transitioning to H-1B employment.

Cap-exempt filings would be spared. Petitions filed by institutions of higher education, affiliated nonprofit organizations, and government research entities would not be subject to the fee, preserving a longstanding distinction in immigration law.

Technology companies and employers in engineering and software development would bear the heaviest burden, according to the Society for Human Resource Management. These sectors rely disproportionately on H-1B workers and would see hiring costs surge by orders of magnitude.

What This Means for Indian Workers

Indian nationals consistently account for more than 70 percent of all H-1B visas issued annually, making this community by far the most affected by the proposed fee. For an Indian software engineer whose employer files an H-1B petition, the $103,265 fee — on top of existing filing costs, legal fees, and premium processing charges — could push the total cost of sponsorship well beyond $120,000.

The economics could fundamentally alter hiring decisions. Smaller companies and startups that currently sponsor H-1B workers may find the cost prohibitive, potentially concentrating skilled immigration sponsorship among only the largest corporations that can absorb the expense.

What Happens Next

The public comment period for the proposed rule runs approximately 30 days, with comments due around September 24, 2026. Immigration attorneys and industry groups are expected to mount significant opposition during the comment period, arguing that the fee is disproportionate and designed to suppress legal immigration rather than fund agency operations.

The next H-1B cap season begins in spring 2027, and the proposed rule's timeline suggests the administration aims to have the regulation in place before then. However, the rulemaking process typically takes months, and legal challenges are virtually certain.

The temporary fee imposed by executive order expires in September 2026, creating a gap the administration is racing to fill with this permanent regulation. Whether courts will view the regulatory approach more favorably than the executive order remains an open question — but for hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals and their employers, the stakes could not be higher.
